project: Hays Grass ID Lab — reusable botanical reference intake

source.title: The Grasses of Texas
source.author: Frank W. Gould
source.illustrations: Drawings by Valloo Kapadia and others
source.bibliographic_url_note: Publisher's later 2000 paperback listing; the user photographed an older cover, and the exact printing of their copy is unverified. First publication of the original work: 1975.

source_intake.material: User-photographed cover and a Schizachyrium scoparium species treatment
source_intake.preservation: Paraphrased provenance and observations, not copyrighted page-image bytes; further species require supplied relevant taxon pages

source_use_policy: Use alongside Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015) for vegetative characters and Diggs et al. (1999) for regional and reproductive characters. Do not discard previous evidence or silently resolve conflicting morphology. Historical taxon concepts, ranges, and chromosome reports are descriptive, not automatic Hays County voucher/nativity proof. Add new trait scoring only when option meaning matches the correct organ and supporting evidence.

observations.details: Cespitose perennial; may be without rhizomes or have rhizomes. Already represented as tufted with possible short underground stems; Gould does not justify a spreading-only score.
Culms described from 50 to 200 cm; this is a broad published range and not a hard rejection criterion.
Culms green or glaucous, freely branching in their upper portion and bearing numerous flowering branches. Branching already scored; color and abundance are new contextual details.

Sheaths strongly keeled and laterally compressed, as broad as 10 mm in some plants but usually considerably narrower. Hairiness ranges from glabrous to villous-pubescent. Existing sheath form and conditional hair mapping retained.
Ligules firm, 1–3 mm long. Matches already source-scored membranous firm ligule; Gould text alone does not separately restate the ligule membrane/edge form in this excerpt.

Basal blades mainly 1.5–4 mm wide, rarely as broad as 6 mm, and 25 cm or longer; linear-tapering with hairiness from smooth to sparse stiff hairs or villous. Width and variable hairiness already represented; minimum length newly retained.
Short flowering racemes mostly 2.5–5 cm long; their architecture is already a primary key clue, numeric interval now retained as a Gould reference.

Rachis joints and pedicels with long silvery cilia at least on the upper two-thirds of these structures. Earlier evidence mapped hairs to the partner stalk; this adds distribution and color without asserting hairs on the spikelet itself.
Sessile spikelets usually 6–8 mm; first glume glabrous or scabrous. True lemma/awn should not be confused with the stalked spikelet partner.

Pedicelled spikelets staminate or neuter, from equal in length to the sessile ones to much shorter; either awnless or bearing a short straight awn. This describes the pedicelled partner, NOT the fertile sessile spikelet awn.
Gould reports 2n=40; cytological report only, not a field-identification or Hays population certification.

Gould's line explicitly says 'lemma 8–15 mm long.' Its organ interpretation requires source reconciliation with other treatments; do NOT silently recode this as true-lemma length or true lemma-awn length.
Only the beginning of the var. divergens couplet is visible below the treatment; the full key was not supplied, and no local subspecies/variety assignment is supported.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the plant and its lower leaves (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould reports stems about 50–200 cm tall, green or bluish-waxy (glaucous); basal leaves typically 1.5–4 mm wide (rarely 6 mm) and 25 cm or longer. Stems may branch repeatedly above. These broad ranges are supporting clues, not exclusive limits.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: season, site conditions, and multiple plants; other grasses overlap these sizes
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published Texas flora description, not verified for a local specimen; retain variation.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Schizachyrium scoparium account (photographed page number not visible)

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the short raceme and its silvery hairs (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Racemes are mostly 2.5–5 cm long. Their rachis joints and pedicels bear long silvery hairs over at least the upper two-thirds. Sessile spikelets are usually 6–8 mm long, with a first glume that may be smooth or rough. Look at intact flowering material with a hand lens.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: silky-haired rachis joints and pedicels versus hairs actually on the spikelet or distant culm nodes
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould's published anatomical measurements; no newly verified macrophotograph.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Schizachyrium scoparium account (photographed page number not visible)

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check which paired spikelet has the awn (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The pedicelled partner may be staminate or neuter and as long as or shorter than the sessile spikelet; its awn can be absent or short and straight. This does NOT mean the fertile sessile spikelet lacks a true awn. Sheaths may be strongly keeled and laterally flattened, up to 10 mm broad but usually narrower.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: upper fertile lemma awn on the sessile spikelet; do not score the pedicelled partner's short awn as the fertile one
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould treatment corroborates the separate-anatomy caution. No automatic key-state changes.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Schizachyrium scoparium account (photographed page number not visible)

additional_species_treatments.illustration: Fig. 84, Elymus virginicus inflorescence; credited in Gould to Gould and Box (1965)
additional_species_treatments.material: Owner photograph showing printed page 166 and attached engraving, not an independently measured wild specimen

head_decision.rationale: Elymus spikelets sit directly along one unbranched inflorescence axis and their straight/weakly curved lemma awns make the whole spike appear bristly. This is NOT the foxtail/Setaria type of bristles from sterile branchlets below spikelets; compact bristly appearance alone is not evidence of a foxtail panicle.
head_decision.visual_qualifier: Typically stiffly erect even at maturity; the existing 'upright or nodding' category describes the broader single-spike group, not nodding Virginia wildrye specifically.

observations.source_statement: Tufted culms, strictly erect or decumbent at base, mostly 60–120 cm tall; green to glaucous.
observations.details: Habit and culm posture were already characterized in existing evidence. Gould independently corroborates the overall range; a decumbent basal culm does not mean the inflorescence nods.
Gould gives a glabrous condition; H&L permits occasional hairiness. Retain source-specific variation rather than erase the previous conditional character.
Consistent with the existing membranous-ligule core state; H&L gives a more specific 0.5–1-mm range and possible fine marginal cilia.

observations.source_statement: Flat, glabrous, scabrous, or minutely pubescent; mostly 5–15 mm broad.
observations.details: Matches existing flat blade and measured 5–15-mm width. Skin roughness and fine hairs are variable, not obligatorily absent.

observations.source_statement: Spike usually stiffly erect, often partially enclosed by the upper leaf sheath.
observations.details: Primary basis for keeping 'spike' and clarifying that wheat/rye-like spikes can appear bristly due to awns. This is a single unbranched main axis, not a foxtail panicle.

observations.source_statement: Strongly nerved, indurate, yellowish glumes bowed outward at a nerveless base, with often somewhat curved apex.
observations.details: Hardened, pale U-like expanded glume bases are diagnostic comparative anatomy; a single node alone does not establish species identity where hybrids may occur.

observations.source_statement: Glume apex tapers to a straight awn shorter to longer than the glume body.
observations.details: GLUME awn, not lemma awn; do not conflate their measurement or infer a fixed awn/body ratio.
Variable smooth-to-sparsely-hairy lemma, not necessarily a conspicuously hairy lemma.

observations.source_statement: Straight or slightly curved lemma awn 5–25 mm long.
observations.details: These are TRUE lemma awns, not foxtail's separate sterile branchlet bristles. Relatively shorter/straighter than typical Canada wildrye, but can still be conspicuous. Existing 5–25-mm score evidence preserved.
Published cytological number; not field-identification evidence or proof for a particular Hays specimen.

observations.source_statement: In Gould's 1975 region scheme, occasional in Texas regions except 9 and 10 and more abundant in the eastern half; shaded banks, fence rows and open woodlands.
observations.details: Historical broad distribution/habitat only; NOT modern BONAP Hays County nativity or a local voucher.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Is it a true erect bristly spike or a foxtail?
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes a stiffly erect spike, often partly tucked into the upper leaf sheath. Follow the actual head axis: Elymus spikelets attach directly to it, with straight or slightly curved lemma awns giving the bristly outline. This is not the separate sterile branchlet bristles of a Setaria foxtail.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Setaria foxtails (separate bristles beneath spikelets) and Canada wildrye (often nodding spikes and longer divergent awns)
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published Texas flora p. 166 plus Texas A&M and USDA descriptions; no identification of a new local specimen.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Elymus virginicus treatment, printed p. 166

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check the U-shaped glume bases and straight awns
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: At mature spikelet nodes, inspect the firm, often yellowish, strongly veined glumes; their bases bow outward and lack veins. Gould reports the true lemma awns as straight or slightly curved, 5–25 mm long, with lemmas hairless or sparsely hairy.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Canada wildrye often has sharper V-shaped glumes and longer, outward-curving lemma awns; hybrids can be intermediate.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-specific diagnostic features, not a specimen-vouchered determination.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Elymus virginicus treatment, printed p. 166

additional_species_treatments.audit_hold: Do not map bristly silhouette to foxtail; retain original head='spike', original awn classifications, photo credits and saved conditional variation. No original printed page photograph is rehosted.

additional_species_treatments.illustration_reference: Fig. 294 cited in treatment, not pictured in this submitted page
additional_species_treatments.material: Owner photograph of Gould's Cenchrus key fragment above the Cenchrus ciliaris species account, plus visible distribution and flowering period

classification_decision.rationale: A dense cylindrical bristly inflorescence supports a foxtail-like outward appearance. Buffelgrass fascicle bristles are mostly fused only at the base and are distinct from lemma/glume awns. Current research-trial head/awn categorization can remain until original-key promotion evidence is independently reconciled.
classification_decision.ligule_note: The book says short CILIATE MEMBRANE with hairs 1–1.5 mm: this is a membranous structure carrying marginal hairs, not evidence for a hair-only ligule. Preserve the current unknown core ligule slot until source-specific mapping and organism-wide candidate promotion is reviewed.
classification_decision.nativity_note: Gould calls it introduced forage grass; do not treat its reported Texas presence or one Hays occurrence as native county flora.

observations.details: Original treatment names Cenchrus ciliaris L. and synonym Pennisetum ciliare (L.) Link. Do not assume any extra synonym or cultivar based on this page.
Perennial; stems erect or knee-bent and spreading, branched and described as 'knotty' at base. Growth form is NOT established from the available research-trial photographs.
Stems 50–100 cm tall in this historical Texas treatment.
Sheaths laterally compressed and keeled, from hairless to sparsely pilose.

Short, ciliate membranous ligule. Gould describes the hairs as mostly 1–1.5 mm long; this is the hair length, NOT an explicit measured height of the membrane itself. Do not transform this into a hair-only ligule score.
Blades thin, usually flat, rough or slightly hairy; mostly 8–30 cm long and 2.5–8 mm broad.
Dense, cylindrical flowering head, mostly 4–10 cm long, occasionally to 13 cm, and 1–2 cm thick. This supports an observational dense bristly cylinder, not a universally identified local specimen.

Purplish bristles 4–10 mm long, cylindrical in cross section (terete), long-ciliate along inner margins, united (connate) only at their bases or slightly above. Separate bristles from glume and lemma awns.
Each fascicle has 2–4 spikelets and a minute, hairy (pilose) peduncle. Count the spikelets inside one bristle-bearing fascicle rather than counting separate fascicles.
Spikelets reported as 2.5–5.6 mm long.
Lemma of the UPPER floret 2.2–5.4 mm long; never map directly to spikelet length or awn length.
Caryopses turgid, ovoid, about 1.4–1.9 mm long and approximately 1 mm in diameter. This describes mature grains, not the entire spikelet.
Gould lists multiple reported chromosome counts, not a specific cytotype confirmed from Hays County.

Gould describes the grass as introduced for forage, then common on sandy rangelands and semi-disturbed sites through Texas region 6, occasionally regions 2, 3, 7, and 10. Historical regional bins are NOT current county-level native distribution.
Gould describes it as native to India and Africa and widely introduced elsewhere. Do not translate this historical generalization into a present-day global distribution determination.
Gould reports flowering from early spring to late autumn under favorable growing conditions. Do not imply a guaranteed Hays County observation window.

adjacent_genus_key_excerpt.scope: Partial Cenchrus key printed immediately ABOVE Cenchrus ciliaris; NOT the C. ciliaris species diagnosis, and the beginning of the key is cut off.

taxa.diagnostic_condition: Burs with one whorl of united flattened spines, subtended by one to several whorls of bristles.
Burs with more than one whorl of flattened spines at irregular intervals; mostly 8–40 spines, larger spine bases often to 1.5 mm wide, upper floret 3.4–5.8 mm.
Burs with more than one whorl of flattened spines at irregular intervals; mostly 45–75 spines, larger spine bases seldom over 1 mm wide, upper floret 5.8–7.6 mm.

adjacent_genus_key_excerpt.caution: Do not apply these spiny-bur species counts as C. ciliaris diagnostic states, and do not treat partial genus couplets as an exhaustive Cenchrus key.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the dense bristly head (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The buffelgrass inflorescence is a close-packed cylinder, mostly 4–10 cm long (sometimes to 13 cm), about 1–2 cm thick. Its purplish bristles are about 4–10 mm and can look foxtail-like, but inspect the bristles and spikelets rather than identifying by the silhouette alone.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Setaria foxtails and other Cenchrus grasses; confirm whether a fascicle's bristles are united near their bases and how many spikelets it encloses.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould published description; Cenchrus ciliaris remains a research trial, with no verified Hays specimen.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas, Cenchrus ciliaris treatment, printed page not visible in photograph

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the ciliate membrane and flattened sheath (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The ligule is a short MEMBRANE with marginal hairs mostly 1–1.5 mm long; this is not a pure fringe-of-hairs ligule. The leaf sheath is flattened and keeled, sometimes bearing sparse hairs; flat blades are mostly 2.5–8 mm wide.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Separate the true membrane from its hairs at the inner blade–sheath junction using magnification; do not measure nearby collar hairs as ligule height.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published Texas flora source. No new core ligule state scored in the provisional identification key.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas, Cenchrus ciliaris treatment, printed page not visible in photograph

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Separate a fascicle and count spikelets (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The bristles are joined only at their bases or a little above. Gould reports 2–4 spikelets per fascicle and spikelets 2.5–5.6 mm long; the UPPER floret lemma is 2.2–5.4 mm. Avoid equating a bristle, a true awn, a fascicle and a spikelet.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Compare whole fascicles with Setaria's separate sterile branchlet bristles and spiny sandbur involucres.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould's organism-specific source measurements; dissection and a source-certified local macrophotograph still needed.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas, Cenchrus ciliaris treatment, printed page not visible in photograph

additional_species_treatments.audit_hold: Keep Cenchrus ciliaris introduced and provisional; no changes to original 112, the optional 1,815-record master, candidate promotion/stock photos/rights or core head/awn/ligule scoring. Historical Texas regions and genus key fragments do not certify Hays nativity or local species ID. Do not host owner-photographed book page image as public source media.

additional_species_treatments.common_name: Ryegrass (per Gould); perennial ryegrass in contemporary field use
additional_species_treatments.illustration_reference: Fig. 51 cited with species name; the actual illustration was not included in supplied photo.
additional_species_treatments.material: User-photographed The Grasses of Texas printed p. 106: Lolium genus description, comparative couplet, and complete visible beginning of Lolium perenne species treatment.

observations.details: Annual grasses or short-lived perennials, normally with succulent culms and flat or folded blades.
Genus description gives membranous ligules, often with thin membranous auricles at blade bases.
Spike of several-flowered spikelets, usually one spikelet per rachis node oriented edgewise against a continuous axis.
Separation described above the glume(s) and between individual florets.
First glume usually absent except at terminal spikelet; second glume generally large, several-veined and awnless. These statements are genus-level architecture, not independent specimen verification.
Lemmas described as 5–9-nerved, rounded on back and either awnless or awned from a generally broad tip.
Gould broadly describes the genus as naturally distributed in temperate Europe and Asia. This does not establish individual species nativity in Hays County.

printed_historical_key.details: Glume shorter than the spikelet; long-lived annual or short-lived perennial under Gould's historical species concept.
Glume extends above the uppermost floret; short-lived annual.

genus_context.cautions: Gould's two-species Texas key is not an exhaustive modern Lolium key. It does not distinguish present-day L. multiflorum, L. × boucheanum or all hybrids. Do not turn a historical genus couplet into a negative Hays species filter.
genus_context.adjacent_unrelated_note: The cropped Festuca paradoxa material above the Lolium heading belongs to a preceding species account and was not assigned to Lolium.

classification_decision.rationale: Gould describes the usual erect, unbranched, two-ranked ryegrass spike. He explicitly allows lemma awns to 8 mm, even though the current provisional evidence says typically awnless. The published variation is saved as a separate claim rather than converting an individual plant to an awned or awnless score. Mature spikelet, same-specimen glumes, presence of hybridization, historical species concepts and planting history remain important.
classification_decision.family_scope_note: Gould genus-level traits must remain distinct from species-only observations. Species remains introduced/unverified Hays County research trial; no evidence promotes to the original 112 scored group or BONAP native inventory.

observations.details: Gould describes annual or short-lived perennial, differing in emphasis from the common perennial ryegrass name. Keep wording as printed rather than silently convert to obligately perennial.
Gould reports no rhizomes or stolons. A decumbent culm or basal bunch does not demonstrate a true runner.
Culms 25–70 cm tall; hairless, fairly thick and succulent when green.
Culms glabrous and fairly thick/succulent when green.
Leaves described as glabrous to scabrous and dark green. Do not infer a required smooth leaf surface from one specimen.
Sheaths often have delicate membranous auricles. Genus description also notes thin membranous auricles; do not require their presence on every leaf.
Upper margins of leaf sheath thin and hyaline (translucent), merging near the blade base into a membranous ligule. This is membrane construction, not a hair-only ligule.
Leaf blades 2–10 mm wide; blades may shrink substantially and lose bulk as they dry.
Blades shrivel when dry; measure and describe fresh or properly rehydrated tissue where practical.
Unbranched flowering spike usually 10–20 cm long.
About 15–30 spikelets, one at each axis node, appressed or somewhat spreading and oriented edgewise relative to rachis. Gould's count is a species description, not a strict threshold.
Mostly 5–12 florets within each spikelet. Earlier Kew research packet lists a wider/different range; keep both source-specific.
First glume generally absent except at the terminal spikelet. Compare node position before interpreting single glume status.
Glumes about 5–10 mm long and 1/3–2/3 as long as spikelet with 3–7 strong veins; don't confuse their length with awn or entire spikelet length.
Lemmas approximately as long as glumes and reported five-nerved, with veins generally obscure except toward margins/apex.

Gould explicitly permits either awnless lemmas with blunt membranous tips or lemmas carrying awns up to 8 mm arising from a minutely notched tip. Do NOT automatically assign both positive and negative main-key states or ignore possible taxonomic/hybrid overlap; review anatomical species concept and local voucher first.
Paleas described as about as long as lemmas, with rough (scabrous) surfaces or short hairs (ciliate) along veins.
Gould reports 2n=14; historical literature report only, not a cytological voucher of a Hays population.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the edge-on spikelets up the ryegrass spike (Gould p. 106)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: An unbranched spike about 10–20 cm long usually bears 15–30 edge-on spikelets, each at a node along the rachis. Gould reports about 5–12 florets in a spikelet. Look at actual attached nodes: this is a spike, not a foxtail made of separate sterile bristles.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Virginia wildrye has conspicuous glume/lemma awns; L. multiflorum and L. × boucheanum can look similar to L. perenne.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould 1975, printed p. 106; literature-only profile, no locally verified voucher.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas (1975), printed p. 106, Lolium perenne

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check the glume, floret and lemma tip together (Gould p. 106)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The first glume is normally missing except on the tipmost spikelet; other glumes are usually 5–10 mm long with 3–7 strong veins. Gould describes L. perenne as generally awnless but also allows a lemma awn up to 8 mm from a minutely notched tip. Do not automatically rule the species in or out by awns alone.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Compare whole-spikelet glume proportions, true lemma awns and leaf auricles with L. multiflorum and hybrids; the old L. temulentum couplet is not a complete modern key.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-specific variation with species/hybrid interpretation held; identification must use multiple characters.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas (1975), printed p. 106, Lolium perenne

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Look closely at the pale membranous collar and soft stems (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Membranous ligule at the inner leaf collar; delicate transparent sheath margins and often tiny membranous auricles. Gould gives 2–10 mm leaf width, 25–70 cm glabrous green culms and a blade that shrivels conspicuously when dried. Paleas may be rough or minutely hairy on their veins.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: A short translucent ligule and clasping ears are different anatomical structures. These supporting clues overlap with other Lolium.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published Texas species account; supplemental teaching clues, not new scored states.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas (1975), printed p. 106, Lolium perenne

additional_species_treatments.audit_hold: Historical treatment, no evidence of a local native Hays voucher. Keep all original 112 data, research trial statuses and current core/optional scores unchanged; preserve possible awned variants separately from modern typical awnlessness, and do not publish a book page scan or unsourced inferred photograph.

additional_species_treatments.illustration_reference: Fig. 81 cited in the treatment, not visible in this supplied photograph
additional_species_treatments.material: Owner photograph of Frank W. Gould, The Grasses of Texas, printed p. 160; original Hordeum leporinum treatment and opening of distribution, with preceding Hordeum jubatum material not assigned to this taxon

taxonomic_crosswalk.verification_status: Kew POWO AND USDA ARS GRIN AGREE
taxonomic_crosswalk.bibliographic_discrepancy: Gould printed Link, Linnaea 9:133, 1835; POWO and GRIN list Link, Linnaea 9:133, 1834. Preserve the original printed date and record the modern bibliographic difference rather than silently rewriting the image.
taxonomic_crosswalk.interpretation: The dated species-level Gould description does not automatically characterize subspp. murinum or glaucum, nor demonstrate which subspecies is represented in existing general H. murinum images and local observation records.
taxonomic_crosswalk.introduced_status: Current Kew distribution treats subsp. leporinum as introduced in Texas. This is not native to Hays County under the project nativity standard, nor proof any individual local record belongs to this subspecies.

classification_decision.reason: Gould's old Hordeum leporinum applies to modern H. murinum subsp. leporinum. Store the morphology on the existing H. murinum research profile with explicit subspecies scoping, not as exclusive states for the entire species complex. No new Hays County subspecies voucher or photo audit.
classification_decision.photo_caution: Existing gallery images labeled H. murinum do not prove subsp. leporinum and should not be relabeled.
classification_decision.history_caution: Gould's historical Texas regional description is not a modern BONAP county occurrence or native-status determination.

observations.details: Gould describes a tufted annual under the name Hordeum leporinum, referring to modern H. murinum subsp. leporinum.
Culms thick, succulent, mostly 15–60 cm tall, usually geniculate-spreading at their lower portions. The bent base is not a nodding flowerhead.
Leaves reported glabrous or more frequently hispid (bearing rather stiff hairs); this must not be recoded as obligatorily hairy.

Ligules truncate (flat-tipped), about 1 mm long. The visible Gould paragraph does not specify ligule construction explicitly, so do not infer a new membrane-versus-hair classification from this sentence alone.
Blades weak and flat, mostly 3–8 mm wide and 6–15 cm long.
Usually with well-developed, slender, pointed auricles at the leaf base; inspect actual clasping structures before deciding their shape.
Flowerhead 4–8 cm long and around 1 cm broad, excluding awns; often partly enclosed in the expanded uppermost leaf sheath.

Florets of lateral spikelets described as large, usually as large as or larger than the floret of the central spikelet. This is Gould's leporinum concept, not necessarily true for every H. murinum subspecies.
Central spikelet floret sits on an elongated rachilla joint about as long as the pedicels of the lateral spikelets; distinguish the rachilla from an actual spikelet pedicel.
Outer glumes associated with the lateral florets are narrow, bristlelike (setaceous), and long-awned. Save printed anatomical wording without conflating glumes and true florets.

Central-spikelet glumes and inner glumes of lateral spikelets are long-awned, broadened/flattened below, with coarse cilia on the margins of that flattened basal portion. A macro photograph is required to confirm that architecture on a specimen.
Glume awns are rough (scabrous), mostly 1–2.5 cm long. Not the 10–35 mm lemma awn described separately.
Lemma BODY 6–12 mm long, gradually tapering to a separate AWN 10–35 mm long. Preserve which organ is being measured; do not add these numbers together as a spikelet length.
Paleas of lateral florets pubescent (hairy), as distinct from lemma or glume hairs.
Stamens of central florets exserted at anthesis (projecting from the flower at flowering time).
Gould reports chromosome number 2n=28; no Hays specimen cytological proof.

Gould says occasional across Texas except the far eastern and southern regions (his regions 1 and 6), and begins describing it as a roadside weed. The remainder continues beyond this photo; no additional habitats should be invented.
Text immediately ABOVE this treatment refers to Hordeum jubatum (foxtail barley), including its separate flowering period and measurements. No Hordeum jubatum traits were assigned to leporinum.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Hare barley within the wall-barley complex — check the triads
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould's historical H. leporinum is now H. murinum subsp. leporinum. In its flowering spike, the lateral florets may equal or exceed the central one. Check central and lateral spikelet structures at several intact rachis nodes; don't assume every H. murinum specimen is this subspecies.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Other H. murinum subspecies and H. pusillum; require same-specimen close-ups of the central and lateral spikelets before identifying below species rank.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould's p. 160 published subsp. leporinum concept plus Kew/USDA name crosswalk; not a locally confirmed subspecies.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p. 160 (as H. leporinum); Kew POWO accepted subsp. leporinum

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Separate flattened, ciliate GLUMES from rough awns
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: For Gould's hare-barley treatment, the central glumes and inner lateral glumes are broadened and flattened below, with coarse hairs on the flattened margin. Glume awns are mostly 10–25 mm and rough; lemma bodies 6–12 mm taper to lemma awns 10–35 mm. These are separate organs, not interchangeable lengths.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Compare bristlelike outer lateral glumes with flattened, hair-margined inner lateral glumes; verify the distinction with a hand lens or macro photo.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-specific published anatomy, not subspecies-confirmed in existing Lab photos.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p. 160, original name Hordeum leporinum

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the leaf collar and compact seedhead
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould reports a tufted annual, stems mostly 15–60 cm tall, flat blades 3–8 mm wide and 6–15 cm long, a truncate ligule around 1 mm, and usually narrow pointed auricles. The flowering head is about 4–8 × 1 cm excluding awns, often partly sheltered by the uppermost sheath. These are for subsp. leporinum specifically.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not treat a roughly bristly Hordeum head or general H. murinum gallery photo as a proven hare-barley subspecies record.

genus_context.source_boundary: The image begins mid-genus description; genus introduction is incomplete. The intact visible two-choice comparison and historical notes are saved, not an exhaustive key.
genus_context.historical_general_context: Gould describes approximately 30 Triticum species under his historical circumscription, in cool-temperate southern Europe and western Asia, and includes weedy Aegilops formerly treated by others under Aegilops. These historical genus limits are not adopted as modern taxonomy.

historical_two_choice_key.character: Spikelets laterally flattened (compressed from side to side)

modern_name_crosswalk.interpretation: Jointed goatgrass is separate from cultivated wheat and is no longer generally placed in Triticum. The historical genus key cannot be used as an exhaustive modern Triticum versus Aegilops identification key.

genus_context.caution: Do not transfer the cylindrical-spikelet and weedy Aegilops statements to wheat; no additional Aegilops specimen promotion or scoring inferred.

classification_decision.rationale: Awned and awnless wheat forms are both documented. Gould's 1–3 cm ligule length conflicts with Texas botanical sources showing ~1–3 mm; retain the literal cm but HOLD numerical length scoring as possible print error. Introductory cultivated wheat, transient roadsides, and cultivar variation require care; don't admit to Hays native flora.

observations.details: Gould describes wheat as an annual.
Thick culms mostly 60–100 cm tall.
Sheaths thin and rounded; typically hairless but lower sheaths can be finely puberulent.
Usually slender auricles on both sides of the leaf collar.

comparison_sources.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Triticum aestivum
University of Texas Plant Resources Center, Williamson County Triticum aestivum

observations.details: The photographed Gould page visibly prints 'Ligules truncate, mostly 1–3 cm long.' This is preserved VERBATIM as source transcription, NOT treated as a verified 10–30 mm identification trait. Other independent sources report millimetres; likely printing/unit error, but source erratum not established. Ligule membrane type is separately supported by regional sources.
Blades elongated, 0.7–2 cm broad, glabrous or scabrous in Gould's Texas material; dry/young variation not quantified.
Spike 5–12 cm long excluding awns, with closely imbricate spikelets in two ranks along a stout, continuous rachis.
Spikelets mostly 10–15 mm long excluding awns, sometimes glabrous or pubescent, with or without awns.
Gould reports 2–5 florets within spikelets. Do not confuse whole spikelet counts with floret counts.
Spikelets laterally compressed, oriented flatwise to rachis, two-ranked and closely overlapping. The genus couplet contrasts this with old 'Triticum cylindricum' (modern Aegilops cylindrica).
Fragmentation described as above glumes and between florets; continuous stout rachis is not proof that every cultivated form sheds naturally.
Glumes normally strongly keeled toward one side, with keel often ending in a minute point (mucronate) or stout awn.
Gould permits stout glume awns of 6 cm or more; does not require every glume to be awned. Do not conflate glume awn length with fertile lemma awns.
Lemmas keeled or rounded on the back; may be awnless, mucronate, or conspicuously awned.
Gould permits stout, scabrous lemma awns to 15 cm or more; both awned and awnless forms included. This is not a universal phenotype or an absolute species maximum.
Paleas well developed, about as large as lemmas.
Caryopses ovate or oblong, usually pubescent at the apex. This describes grain tip, not the whole spikelet.
Gould describes embryo as roughly one-fourth to one-third the length of the endosperm, not the whole spikelet.
Published 2n=42; do not treat as chromosome certification of Hays roadside plants.

Gould reports wheat as cultivated and collected as a weed on Texas roadsides and waste areas, especially around agriculture, while stating it did not become independently established outside cultivation in his historical observations. This is not a modern Hays naturalization determination.

Gould calls wheat native to Eurasia and widespread as a cultivated plant. Modern Kew describes a cultigen origin more precisely; do not treat the historical broad phrase as a natural wild species range.
Gould gives flowering mostly March to May, not guaranteed site-level timing in Hays County.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Follow the two-ranked wheat spike (Gould p. 173)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes a stiff 5–12 cm flowering spike with closely overlapping, laterally flattened spikelets in two ranks on a stout rachis. Spikelets are usually 10–15 mm (excluding awns) and contain 2–5 florets. Compare several complete mature spikes rather than relying on a single silhouette.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Jointed goatgrass (Aegilops cylindrica; Gould's T. cylindricum) has more cylindrical spikelets; other cereals can overlap in head outline.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published description for cultivated bread wheat; not identification of an individual local escaped plant.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p. 173, Triticum aestivum

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Look at the glume versus lemma awn (Gould p. 173)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: The glume may end in a short point or a stout awn reported to 6 cm or more; the lemma may be awnless, mucronate or have rough stout awns reaching 15 cm or more. This source includes both awned and awnless wheat, so don't force one exclusive awn answer.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Identify the exact bract from which an awn arises, and distinguish the glume keel from a lemma awn. Cultivated forms differ widely.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould source description only; no new scoring of awn length or mandatory awn state.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p. 173, Triticum aestivum

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check collar auricles and the ligule-unit warning
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes slender auricles and a truncate ligule but prints a ligule length of 1–3 cm. Regional botanical floras report millimetres instead (roughly 1–3 mm). Treat Gould's printed centimetre value as ON HOLD, not a measurement to use in identification. Stems are mostly 60–100 cm and leaves 7–20 mm wide.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: A ligule is inside the leaf blade–sheath junction; auricles are different projections on either side. Verify with a scale before applying a length bin.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Printed Gould cm versus external mm sources explicitly disagreed; exact source erratum unconfirmed.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p. 173; Diggs et al. (1999) wheat account; UT PRC Williamson County wheat treatment

additional_species_treatments.audit_hold: Keep Triticum aestivum as non-native research-trial candidate, do not promote from supplied cultivated wheat description. Protect all original 112 source shards, optional 1,815-record evidence master, 57 provisional scoring states, photos and credits. Printed ligule 1–3 cm is a documented conflict and must NOT be used for any filter without resolving edition erratum. Historical Triticum cylindricum belongs to modern Aegilops cylindrica, not wheat. No copyrighted book page is rehosted.

observations.details: Perennial with culms rising from thick, scaly rhizomes; clonal growth is supported, but source does not require true surface stolons.
Erect culms mostly 20–75 cm tall.
Leaves glabrous or essentially glabrous; this is not a claim every individual leaf has no hairs.

Gould describes a dense ring of short hairs; UT Plant Resources Center describes a true membranous truncate ligule approximately 0.2–0.5 mm tall, with hairs above/along its upper side. University of Florida independently characterizes it as a membrane with a fringe of hairs. Preserve Gould's visible ring but do not assume hair-only membrane absence from the 1975 wording.

comparison_refs.authority: UT Plant Resources Center, Williamson County Paspalum notatum
comparison_refs.support: True membranous ligule 0.2–0.5 mm with separate short hairs near the collar

comparison_refs.authority: University of Florida IFAS Florida Turfgrass Identification

observations.details: Blades 2–6 mm broad; may be flat, folded or inward-rolled (involute) and usually firm and tough.
Blades flat, folded or involute, generally firm and tough rather than necessarily permanently flat.

Usually two spicate raceme-like flowering branches near the culm tip, paired at one apex or one somewhat below the other. A third branch is sometimes present below the terminal pair. Not two independent culms.
Spikelets closely imbricated in two rows along the raceme rachis; distinguish this from a general unbranched cereal spike.
Spikelets broadly ovate, elliptic or obovate, glabrous and shiny, about 2.8–3.5 mm long; visual and numeric comparison with P. minus matters.
Lemma of upper (fertile) floret straw-colored; not all bracts or glumes are necessarily this color.
Gould reports 2n=20, 30 and 40; numbers are historical reports, not verified local cytotypes or definitive species filters.

Gould reports Texas regions 1 and 2, introduced as a pasture grass and occasionally along roadsides, ditches and lightly disturbed moist sites; historical region bins do not prove Hays county native status.

Gould calls the species native to Mexico, Central and South America; current Kew POWO's native-range treatment is Peru through Brazil to northern Argentina and lists Texas and Mexico among introduced territories. Preserve both source eras rather than silently replacing Gould's wording.
Historical Texas flowering period June–November; season not guaranteed in Hays County.

historical_variety.original_status: Gould describes an introduced strain/variety found in Texas
historical_variety.published_characters: A large, coarse plant with long blades, mostly 2.8–3 mm spikelets and occasionally one to three extra flowering branches below the terminal pair

current_taxonomic_conflict.alternate_accepted_variety_authority: USDA GRIN and ITIS retain Paspalum notatum var. saurae as an infraspecific taxon

historical_variety.policy: Never assign var. saurae-only coarse/extra-branch traits to every ordinary Paspalum notatum and do not combine Paspalum saurae with the project species without concept reconciliation.

classification_decision.rationale: Existing 57-species trial already has paired racemes and rhizomatous growth hypotheses. The Gould hair ring and current membrane evidence together raise a ligule anatomy issue; no exclusive hair-only classification or new key scoring should be asserted from this page alone.
classification_decision.taxonomy_note: Gould var. saurae must stay distinct from P. notatum common species concept; current Kew treats P. saurae as accepted separate species.
classification_decision.locality_note: Introduced turf/pasture status and county-level nativity require independent review.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Compare the paired bahiagrass branches and shiny spikelets (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Bahiagrass typically has two flower-bearing branches about 4–12 cm long, paired at the stem tip or slightly offset. A third branch occasionally occurs lower down. The closely packed spikelets form two rows, are usually 2.8–3.5 mm long, and are broad, smooth and shiny. Inspect an intact mature branch and several separate spikelets.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum minus can have smaller, less-shiny spikelets and denser low mats; P. conjugatum has much smaller spikelets and stolons.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould's published Texas source treatment, not verified on a same-plant Hays County voucher.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Paspalum notatum treatment (page not visible in source photo)

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Open the inner collar: look for membrane beneath the hairs
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould calls the ligule a ring of short hairs, but UT PRC and UF IFAS describe a tiny membranous ligule with hairs above or along its edge. Do not identify a hair-only ligule until magnification shows whether a membrane is present.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Check the true inner blade–sheath junction, not hairs on the nearby collar or stem node; hair ring and membrane can coexist.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source terminology needs reconciliation; no production ligule scoring change based on this literature-only page.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas; UT Plant Resources Center; UF IFAS

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check for thick scaly rhizomes and avoid confusing varieties
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes rhizomes that are thick and scaly and flowering culms mostly 20–75 cm tall. He also mentions an introduced var. saurae; modern authorities differ about its rank, so don't automatically apply those larger-plant traits to every bahiagrass.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not mistake underground rhizomes for surface stolons; look at the rooted crown. P. conjugatum instead has long leafy stolons.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published morphology; the historical variety requires a separate taxonomic review.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, Paspalum notatum treatment (page not visible in source photo)

observations.details: Perennial with erect stems arising from long, leafy aboveground stolons.
Culms 25–50 cm tall.
Nodes of stolons usually pilose (softly hairy).
Blades thin and flat, usually 8–12 cm long and 5–15 mm wide, smooth or less frequently pilose.
Membranous ligule with a ring of stiff hairs immediately ABOVE it, not necessarily hairs replacing the ligule.
Two flowering racemes paired at culm tip, mostly 5–15 cm long and widely spreading.
Spikelets elliptical, broadly pointed, packed closely along rachis.
Glumes sparsely long-pilose along margins; don't transfer glume-margin hairiness to the bahiagrass glumes.
Upper-floret lemma straw-colored.
Reported 2n=40; not a specimen count.

Gould's regional Texas material was confined to the southern part of region 2, with specimens examined from Cameron County. Current POWO includes Texas in a broader native range but neither proves occurrence in Hays County.
Gould says Texas flowering specimens were collected from September to November; not a statewide phenology guarantee.

additional_species_treatments.audit_hold: Separate species from P. notatum. This adjacent source treatment is outside current 169-species Lab candidate collection and must not be added to scored filters, public gallery, or Hays native roster without independent scope and county verification.

observations.details: Gould explicitly says Paspalum minus is similar to P. notatum.
Culms rarely over 30 cm; rhizomatous bases often form dense mats.
Spikelets 2–2.5 mm long and LESS shiny than P. notatum; comparison, not absolute sheen quantification.
Lower sheaths and leaf blades often hirsute or hispid (hairy/bristly).

Contemporary Kew accepts P. minus and lists Texas in its broad native range, but no Hays County BONAP/voucher claim can be made. Do not turn this partial comparison into a full key profile.

taxonomy.note: Gould's species name is accepted today; older genus combinations are synonyms. Botanical author abbreviation differs in modern standard style, not a new species.

observations.details: Cespitose (tufted) perennial with firm nonrhizomatous base; nonrhizomatous in Gould's treatment is not proof that a photo shows the root system.
Flowering stems 30–100 cm.
Leaves mostly glabrous; lowermost leaves sometimes minutely pubescent.
Thin blades mostly 7–18 mm broad, tapering to a slender point.
Flowerheads at tips of long shoots and on slender peduncles in upper leaf axils, potentially more than one head per plant.
Typically 2–5 slender, widely spaced spicate branches; sometimes only one. FNA and regional published ranges differ; keep source-specific descriptions and do not make counts exclusive.
Flowering branches mostly 4–8 cm long.
Pairs of spikelets on either side of a narrow, flat rachis. 'Pairs' describe spikelets on rachis, not necessarily precisely two flowering branches.
Elliptic or elliptic-obovate spikelets, 2.2–2.6 mm. The FNA broader 2.1–3.3 mm interval is retained separately in existing research.
First glume present on some or most spikelets, generally 1/4–1/3 as long as spikelet. Unlike some other paspalums with no first glume.
Second glume AND lower-floret lemma pubescent, usually carrying brownish glandular blotches. Verify each bract separately in a measured, mature spikelet.
Lemma of upper floret light brown. Color alone does not determine the species.
Gould reports 2n=60; not the chromosome result for any current Hays voucher.
Historical Texas regions 1, 2, 3 and 6, usually moist woods or shaded ditchbanks; Kew lists Texas native at state level, not a BONAP Hays certificate.
Gould reports Florida to Texas and south to Venezuela; a historical generalized geographic treatment.
Gould's broad published flowering window; seasonality varies by site and year.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Look for paired spikelets on 2–5 slender racemes (Gould p. 510)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: A mature tufted rustyseed paspalum commonly has 2–5 widely spaced, slender flowering branches about 4–8 cm long; sometimes only one. Spikelets are arranged in pairs along the flattened narrow branch axis. Examine multiple heads, since FNA uses a different branch-number range.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Distinguish pairs of spikelets from pairs of entire racemes; bahiagrass's usually two apical racemes are a different head organization.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould published morphology p.510; FNA variation retained and no same-local-voucher claim.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p. 510; FNA Paspalum langei

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Dissect the first glume and gland-marked lower floret (Gould)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Spikelets about 2.2–2.6 mm. Gould describes a short first glume present on some or most spikelets, and brownish glandular blotches with short hairs on the SECOND glume and LOWER sterile-floret lemma. Photograph both surfaces separately with a millimeter scale.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not misidentify hair spots on a separate grass or count the fertile upper lemma as the lower lemma.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-specific anatomy still not confirmed by a local same-plant macro view; specimen diagnosis remains provisional.

classification_decision.reason: Existing research describes source-backed branch count with different numeric intervals across Gould/FNA; first glume and glandular spots have not been verified in a local specimen.

taxonomy.note: Species named by Gould is still accepted; do not confuse with P. vaginatum/P. mucronulatum in adjacent key.

observations.details: Culms 30–80(-100) cm; stiffly erect or somewhat knee-bent below, glabrous.
Leaf sheaths have a tuft of long hairs on either side of the collar; these are deciduous as the leaf ages and are NOT the ligule itself.
Ligule a ring of short hairs; distinguish from longer hairs immediately above and the collar tufts.
Hairs 2–4 mm long immediately above ligule at base of blade, not overall ligule height.
Blades 10–20(–30) cm by 1.5–5 mm, flat or involute, with texture different by surface.
Rough/scabrous adaxial (upper) face above the base, smooth abaxial (lower) face.
Tightly or loosely contracted panicle, often short somewhat erect-spreading branchlets; NOT a single true spike or foxtail bristle cylinder.
Panicle generally 12–20 cm long, not plant height.
Pink or purple-tinged at maturity; age and specimen color can vary. Genus key contrasts a white/tawny tightly contracted P. vaginatum-type concept.
Spikelets short-pedicelled or appressed, 6–8 mm long.
Per spikelet 2–3 perfect (fertile/bisexual) florets plus two reduced florets above; do not count the reduced ones as fully fertile.
Glumes broad, smooth, acute or minutely notched/mucronate at tip, generally 3–4 mm.
Lemmas broadly rounded, firm, many-veined; midnerve and margins hairy from base to about middle.
Body of lower lemma 3–4 mm long; not including terminal awns.

Awns 11–15 from the terminal portion of a single lemma, of uneven lengths, longest about 2.5–5 mm. These are true lemma awns, not separate foxtail (Setaria) bristles, and not 11–15 awns per WHOLE panicle.
Paleas slightly longer than the body of the lemma, two-veined, tapering to an acute or sharply pointed tip.
Rudimentary upper florets are similar in structure to perfect lower florets but smaller.
Gould reports 2n=100; no cytological verification of a Hays specimen.
Historical Texas regions 2, 6, 7, 8 and 10; grassy plains, moist road rights-of-way and open valleys. Statewide native status is not equivalent to BONAP Hays County nativity.
Gould reports Texas to Arizona and northern Mexico; contemporary FNA disputed an Arizona source report. Record rather than resolve without specimens.
Published flowering period April through November; not a guaranteed local blooming window.

genus_key_context.scope: Partial genus-level Pappophorum couplet visible immediately before species treatment.

first_choice.name: Pappophorum bicolor
first_choice.details: Panicle pink or purplish at maturity, contracted yet narrow and sometimes spreading-branching; usually two perfect florets; lowest lemma body 3–4 mm.

second_choice.name: Pappophorum vaginatum sensu Gould
second_choice.details: Panicle pale white or tawny, more tightly contracted; usually one perfect floret; lowest lemma body 2–3 mm.

genus_key_context.note: Historical genus key is not an exhaustive modern species key. Authors differ on accepted name P. vaginatum vs P. mucronulatum; both require preserved source concepts.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Count awns from a SINGLE lemma (Gould p. 378)
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: At a mature pappusgrass spikelet, a lower lemma has 11–15 thin, unequal awns, the longest about 2.5–5 mm. The lower lemma's firm body is about 3–4 mm long. These are lemma extensions—not independent foxtail bristles or a count of rays in the entire seedhead.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Other Pappophorum and bristly Cenchrus/Setaria grass heads. Use a dissection and close photograph of one lemma.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould p.378, supported by Kew GrassBase; not verified in current Hays specimen photo.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p.378

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Compare pink contracted panicles and two or three perfect florets
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes a 12–20 cm contracted, pink- or purple-tinged panicle whose 6–8 mm spikelets contain 2–3 perfect florets and two reduced apical florets. Check the florets individually rather than judging only pink color.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Gould's P. vaginatum concept has pale, more tightly contracted panicles and generally one perfect floret, but current authorities disagree on its accepted name.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Historical source comparison with contemporary taxon hold; same-plant specimen not established.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p.378

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Separate collar hairs from the true hair ligule
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: This species has collar hair tufts on the sheath sides that can fall off with age, a ring of short hairs as the ligule, and longer 2–4 mm hairs at the blade base above it. Those are three distinct hair positions; do not measure the long blade-base hairs as ligule height.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Compare newly developed and aging leaf collars; preserve hair locations without forcing a membrane-type call from distant photos.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould p.378 morphology corroborated by Texas A&M and FNA field descriptions.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, p.378

observations.details: Tufted perennial; short rhizomes at base (subrhizomatous).
Culms up to about 50 cm.
Lower sheaths pilose, upper sheaths glabrous.
Ligule about 0.8 mm, no explicit construction in this page.
Blades 6–7 mm wide, ciliate on lower margins.
Two terminal racemes with spikelets in two rows widely separated along branches, not overlapping.
Spikelets plano-convex, elliptic and blunt, puberulent.
First glume absent in Gould's P. separatum description.
Gould knew the taxon from type near Golden, Wood County, Texas, on gray silty clay and chalk gravel; this reflects historical material, NOT the broad modern taxon's only range.
Historical type specimen collected in flower in July.

classification_decision.reason: Outside present 169-species research set; modern POWO treats as P. setaceum var setaceum. Do not transfer narrow type-derived characteristics wholesale.

observations.details: Robust perennial from long, stout, scaly rhizomes; stems singly or in small groups.
Culms about 50–120 cm tall.
Leaves otherwise smooth except long-ciliate ligule; read cautiously because hair structures are only partly visible in photo.
Blades inrolled, about 2 mm wide when inrolled; lower blades mostly 20–30 cm or more.
One to three, sometimes four, densely flowering spicate branches.
Branches generally 10–25 cm, sometimes 8–30 cm.
Spikelets usually in pairs with one subsessile and one pedicelled; continuation about pedicel is truncated at edge of photo.
